stature.source: typical and tall: the drafter's estimate for the Sierra (the Gymnosperm Database gives the species to 60 m and calls the Sierra form very large); record: 81 m near Pollock Pines, El Dorado County (Gymnosperm Database; unverified lidar trees of 80-83 m in Del Norte County); read 2026-11-04

targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-04), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a spire somewhat broader and softer than red fir's, branches flat to drooping, shade-grown trees keeping live limbs low

description: A big fir, 25-55 m here, with long, flat, pale silvery-green needles in two soft ranks along the twigs, a spire-shaped crown that flattens with age, and ash-grey bark that thickens into deep, corky furrows. It is the most common tree of the mixed conifer forest of the west slope, about 1200-2400 m, growing in the shade of sugar and ponderosa pines and incense cedar until it fills the understory where fire has been kept out.

season_notes.winter: Evergreen; young firs in the understory bend under the snow and spring back.
season_notes.spring: Soft pale new shoots in May-June; small reddish pollen cones under the lower branches.
season_notes.summer: Upright olive to purple cones stand on the top of the crown.
season_notes.fall: The cones break up on the tree and scatter winged seed in September-October.

range.where: the mixed conifer forest of the west slope: Yosemite Valley rim, Crane Flat, Wawona, Hetch Hetchy, below the red fir

notes: The Sierra form (var. or subsp. lowiana) has needles without the strong white bloom of the Rocky Mountain white fir, so it reads pale grey-green rather than blue; the colour here sits between the template's green and red fir's blue, and paler than both. Bark is the clearest field mark against red fir: grey and corky with yellowish-brown in the furrows, never red-purple. Needles are longer (to about 6 cm) and lie flatter in two ranks than red fir's, which a crown at game distance cannot show. Fire exclusion has made dense thickets of young white fir under the pines; the species mix should allow that. Seeds feed chickarees, chipmunks and nutcrackers (not in the library). The elevation belt is the drafter's knowledge (species range-wide 900-3400 m, Gymnosperm Database).
